analysis_notes.torah_text_coverage: Torah LM2 #70 is an extremely brief teaching — three sentences. It states a single general principle: 'Whoever is greater must seek their desired thing (מְבֻקָּשׁוֹ) at a greater distance.' This is proven by analogy through the hierarchy of creation: the plant (הַצּוֹמֵחַ) receives its vitality immediately from the earth; the animal (בְּהֵמָה), being on a higher level, must seek its food at a slightly greater distance; the human being (בֶּן-אָדָם), being higher still, must seek even farther. The practical proof is Moses (מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ), who — being of the highest spiritual stature — had to seek his wife from distant Midian (מִדְיָן). The text contains NO explicit bechina language (no 'X הוא בְּחִינַת Y', no 'נִקְרָא', no equivalence formulas). The structure is entirely analogical-proportional: greatness of level implies distance of the sought-after thing. This is a proportional relationship (the greater the level, the farther the מבוקש), not an identity or parallel-nature statement. The dataset correctly contains zero bechina edges for reference 1070. There are no missing concepts and no orphaned nodes.
analysis_notes.evil_mirror_note: This Torah has no evil domain. The teaching operates entirely in the register of spiritual levels and cosmic structure — it is a neutral observation about how greatness works in creation. There is no mention of an opposing force, sitra achra, or evil counterpart. No evil mirror package exists.

analysis_notes.structural_note: The teaching's core relationship — גְּדֻלָּה (greatness) proportional to רִחוּק הַמְּבֻקָּשׁ (distance of the sought-after thing) — is a cause-effect/proportional relationship, not a bechina identity. Greatness does not 'share the same nature' as distance; rather, greatness NECESSITATES distance. This is eitza-type logic (the greater one is, the more one must seek far), not bechina-type logic (two names for the same thing). Encoding this as a bechina edge would misrepresent the teaching's structure.
